title: Microscopic Origin of Spin Splitting in Altermagnetic CrSb Thin Films
authors: Dai Mingyang, Song Hongquan, Kang Zhuo, Xu Yuanji, Tian Fuyang
abstract: Altermagnets have recently emerged as promising materials for spintronic applications owing to their momentum-dependent spin splitting. Among them, metallic CrSb is particularly attractive owing to its giant spin splitting and high Néel temperature. However, the microscopic origin of the distinct spin-splitting behaviors in bulk and thin-film CrSb remains unresolved. Here, we systematically investigate the electronic structures of CrSb slabs with different surface orientations using first-principles calculations. Although all considered slabs preserve spin-group symmetries compatible with altermagnetism, they exhibit markedly different electronic structures: the (2$\bar{1}\bar{1}$0) slab retains pronounced altermagnetic spin splitting, whereas the (0001) and (10$\bar{1}$0) slabs display nearly spin-degenerate bands. We demonstrate that dimensional reduction fundamentally changes the microscopic origin of altermagnetic spin splitting. Unlike bulk CrSb, altermagnetic spin splitting in thin films requires long-range inter-unit-cell coplanar Cr--Sb hopping, while Sb--Sb hopping provides an additional contribution. The preservation or suppression of these hopping pathways explains the strong surface dependence of the spin splitting. Our findings establish a microscopic mechanism for understanding altermagnetism in reduced dimensions and provide a general principle for engineering spin splitting in low-dimensional altermagnetic materials.
summary: This work uses first-principles calculations to map the microscopic origin of spin splitting in altermagnetic CrSb thin films. The authors find that surface termination is crucial, showing that robust spin splitting requires specific long-range inter-unit-cell hopping pathways unique to certain surfaces. This establishes a general principle for controlling electronic properties by engineering low-dimensional crystal interfaces.
main_problem: The study aims to resolve the microscopic origin of spin splitting in altermagnetic CrSb thin films, specifically investigating how this property changes when dimensionality is reduced from bulk to 2D.
main_result: The paper demonstrates that surface orientation dictates the electronic structure; while the (2$ ar{1} ar{1}0$) slab retains strong spin splitting, others do not. This splitting fundamentally relies on long-range inter-unit-cell coplanar Cr--Sb hopping pathways.
method: First-principles calculations were used to model CrSb slabs with various surface orientations and varying vacuum spacings to simulate dimensional reduction. Wannier tight-binding Hamiltonians were constructed to analyze the contribution of different hopping channels.
model_or_system: The physical system is metallic CrSb, an altermagnet known for its giant spin splitting. The model involves constructing slab geometries with specific surface terminations ((2$ ar{1} ar{1}0$), (0001), etc.) and systematically varying the inter-slab vacuum spacing to tune coupling strength.
key_observables: Momentum-dependent spin splitting magnitude, electronic band structures along high-symmetry k-paths, and the contribution of specific hopping parameters ($	ext{Cr–Sb}$, $	ext{Sb–Sb}$).
important_parameters: Dimensionality (3D bulk vs. 2D thin film limit), surface orientation, and inter-unit-cell coupling strength.
main_assumptions: The calculations assume that the electronic structure can be accurately modeled by analyzing the contributions of specific hopping pathways derived from first-principles results.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structures for different planes, show the evolution of spin splitting as vacuum spacing changes (comparing surfaces), and detail how retaining specific inter-unit-cell hopping terms is necessary to reproduce the observed spin splitting in the most stable surface orientation.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the electronic structure of bulk vs. various slab geometries using first-principles calculations, then refines this analysis by constructing Wannier Hamiltonians and analyzing the necessity of specific long-range hopping terms ($	ext{Cr–Sb}$ vs $	ext{Sb–Sb}$) to explain the observed spin splitting in low dimensions.
why_interesting: While focused on magnetism, understanding how crystal symmetry and dimensionality fundamentally alter electronic band structure via orbital hybridization (hopping) provides a generalizable principle for engineering quantum properties in novel materials systems.
